About

Hi, I'm Juliana.

“They were short on investment, not talent.”

Every morning on my way to work as a strategy consultant at the World Bank, I walked under a sign that read “Eradicate Poverty,” just minutes after passing people living on the street. I had arrived there fresh from internships in Congress and the DNC, where I drafted travel briefs for President Obama. I believed deeply in these institutions, yet found it strange that the people actually living the problems were never consulted. So I stepped outside to talk to them.

I learned that about 40% of homeless youth had aged out of foster care. Many of the young people I met survived by hustling and already possessed the core skills of business: they could sell, negotiate, and take risks. They were short on investment, not talent. I founded Street Entrepreneurs in 2015 to change that. We started in shelters and juvenile detention centers before moving to the Inclusive Innovation Incubator, opening our doors to anyone with grit and firsthand experience of the problem they wanted to solve.

I ran it like a product, not a charity. The problem was access to the capital, customers, and expertise that founders' own networks couldn't reach. Every workshop, pitch night, and app was a bet on closing that gap, and I measured what worked. Letting parents bring their kids changed who showed up. Letting peers pick the finalists changed who got the stage. In four years, the accelerator grew 60x and earned its largest city grant yet.

The plan rarely survived contact with reality, and adapting was the job. When COVID-19 erased our eight-ward neighborhood accelerator, we rebuilt it online and reached a thousand founders. The peer skill exchange only worked if the right people were in the room, so I built Talent Hive, letting early users drive the roadmap. During the lockdown, when founders' storefronts closed, I built Street Collectiv so neighbors could keep shopping, subscribing, and showing up for the businesses on their block.

That is still how I build: start with the people living the problem, define the hypothesis, ship the simplest version, and pivot when the data demands it. I paired that field instinct with formal frameworks through a master's in Digital Product Management and a Columbia MBA. Today, AI adds the execution speed, turning a written PRD into a live product in days.

For nine years, product was one of the many roles I played as a founder. Now I want it to be my core focus, as part of a dedicated product team. If you're looking for a PM who spots where a product is leaving its users behind, rallies a team around a single vision, prioritizes what matters most, and ships what they need fast, I'd love to talk. I work in English, Spanish, and Portuguese.

Ventures

One accelerator, three ventures, one thesis.

Every company I founded or led set out to build a grit-based economy, a system where grit is the only prerequisite and everything else can be earned. Each digital product addressed a specific problem the accelerator's founders were facing.

While launching these ventures, I became Co-President of Beacon DC, a sister organization for women founders, lectured at UVA Darden Executive Education and Howard University's Executive Education, and consulted on design thinking and innovation.

Testing the thesis across the accelerator's pillars

i. Knowledge
Workshops: practitioner-led, pay-what-you-can

Founders paid what they could to learn from over 80 lecturers. When COVID-19 hit in 2020, a $175,000 city grant allowed us to take the series online. We shipped 70 virtual sessions and distributed Wi-Fi stipends, keeping more than 1,000 founders building through the lockdown.

Watch the recorded workshops
ii. Connections
Talent Exchange: trade skills, and meet experts

An in-person mentorship exchange pairing peer skill-bartering with two expert tracks: coaches for execution and advisors for industry knowledge. This program laid the groundwork for Talent Hive in 2017, and a hybrid version supported 53 businesses in 2020.

iii. Capital
Street Pitch: capital and customers, live and online

I created and produced Street Pitch, an "American Idol meets Shark Tank" showcase connecting founders with capital and customers. Peers selected the founders, judges acted as advisors, and audiences backed them with crowdfunding and purchases. We simulcast the live show through 50+ partner organizations to a combined following of over 300,000, complete with ASL interpretation. For many of our founders, Street Pitch gave them the friends-and-family round their own networks could not provide.

Read the Street Pitch record

One-on-one coachingBeyond directing the program, I coached founders one-on-one, partnering with them to scope, build, and launch their MVPs and design their go-to-market strategies.

Who we built for

  • Designed for inclusion: letting parents bring their children raised women's participation from 20% to 58% within months.
  • A snapshot (2018): 385+ early-stage founders: 50% Black, 20% Latinx, 58% women, 13% LGBTQ+ and 52% first-generation. 1 in 4 worked 60+ hours a week.
  • Verified outcomes: Deloitte's study of 200 participants counted 260 jobs, 134 local value chains, and 84% of founders reporting stronger leadership.

Advocacy

The BEST Act: With a Booz Allen Race and Social Equity grant, I surveyed the rules keeping DC street vendors informal. Backed by 50 interviews and 196 signatures, I testified before the DC Council in 2022, delivering the sole testimony focused on street vending. The BEST Act took effect in 2025, consolidating more than 100 business license categories into 13, removing the regulatory friction that kept founders and street vendors out of the formal economy.

BEST Act case study

Street Entrepreneurs was funded and supported by the DC government, Capital One, Target, Lyft, Amazon Web Services, Deloitte, and 1,000+ individual donors, and covered by the Washington Business Journal, WTOP, Technical.ly (2018, 2019), and Rantt Media. To go deeper, watch this video, read the brochure, or visit streetentrepreneurs.org.

Three ventures

Each one a digital product built to solve a problem founders faced.

Talent HiveFounder and CEO
2017 to 2018

Born from the Talent Exchange.

The problem: founders had skills to trade but no cash to pay for help.

With our CTO, Cory Lancaster, I turned the Talent Exchange program into a time-bank web app: give an hour of your expertise, earn an hour of someone else's. When one founder trained another, they earned Karma Coins to trade for services on the platform, so expertise kept moving without cash. The beta launched in 2018 across DC, Maryland, and Virginia.

Result: 100+ beta users and 128 beta tests in 2.5 months. Their feedback set the V2 roadmap: native iOS and Android apps, in-app chat, and a Spanish version.

Street Investors ExchangeCo-Founder and COO
2018 to 2019

Born from founders' lack of access to capital.

The problem: Many underrepresented founders fell into the blind spots of traditional capital, and the people who did believe in them were not accredited.

We built a gamified investor education platform to drive capital toward women, people of color, and middle America. It tracked top performers and connected them with funds so they could invest locally in their own communities. I led the execution from end to end, driving the product requirements, A/B testing, and the beta launch.

Result: This foundational product work culminated in a 2018 U.S. provisional patent application. Today, the rebuilt platform operates as a risk-free educational simulation.

Street CollectivFounder and CEO
2020 to 2021
Visible Hands VC Fellow, 2021

Born when COVID-19 closed our founders' doors.

The problem: When lockdowns hit Washington, Street Entrepreneurs' founders lost their customers overnight. Most had no way to sell online, nor did their businesses qualify for federal aid, leaving local customer support as their only lifeline.

To solve this, I founded Street Collectiv, an online marketplace that kept neighbors buying from the small businesses on their block. Stephano Muro later joined as co-founder. Owners pre-sold gift cards and services while we handled the digital infrastructure and marketing. I drove the execution from end to end, running the UX research, building the Figma prototypes, and writing the PRDs.

The startup raised capital from Visible Hands VC, and I was selected for their inaugural fellowship (from 900+ applicants). We eventually piloted a “shop of shops” where customers could shop, subscribe, and socialize with small businesses block by block. Our subscription model was intended to steady cash flow and allow small businesses to cement their local community relationships.

Result: a 25% average sales lift for the shops that joined.

Beacon DCCo-President
The D.C. Women Founders Initiative

A sister organization that joined forces with Street Entrepreneurs.

Beacon started as a community-led campaign, launched in November 2016 with the DC Mayor's Office, Google and Georgetown Law's Institute for Technology Law and Policy, with one goal: make D.C. the most influential and supportive city for women entrepreneurs. I served as one of its Co-Presidents from 2020 to 2024.

What we built:

The Directory

Developed the largest directory of women entrepreneurs and support organizations in the District.

Micro-Grants

Directed the distribution of 30 micro-grants to women-led organizations.

Policy Advocacy

Contributed to a widely cited report presented before the U.S. Senate Small Business Committee.

Program Scale

Scaled programs to reach and support more than 600 women founders.
